subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Ceres: Queen of the Asteroid Belt
description: A 60-second lesson on Ceres: Queen of the Asteroid Belt.

hook.text: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt. When discovered in 1801, it was called a planet.

buildup.text: For 50 years, Ceres was listed next to Mars and Jupiter. Then astronomers found too many similar objects.

discovery.text: NASA's Dawn spacecraft found bright salt deposits on Ceres—remnants of a subsurface ocean.

twist.text: Ceres may still have liquid water beneath its crust, making it a surprising target in the search for life.

climax.text: Reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, Ceres joined Pluto in the new category.

punchline.text: Planet, asteroid, dwarf planet. Ceres keeps changing labels.

quiz.question: What surprising feature did NASA's Dawn spacecraft find on Ceres?
options: Bright salt deposits suggesting a subsurface ocean
Active volcanoes erupting from its surface
A dense atmosphere of nitrogen gas

details.summary: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system. At 940 km in diameter, it contains about a third of the belt's total mass. NASA's Dawn spacecraft revealed bright salt deposits, evidence of a subsurface ocean, and possible cryovolcanic activity.
details.whyItMatters: Ceres is a bridge between rocky asteroids and icy moons. Its subsurface ocean makes it an unexpected candidate for astrobiological interest — liquid water exists in a place nobody expected to find it.
takeaways: Ceres is the asteroid belt's largest object at 940 km diameter
Dawn spacecraft found bright salt deposits and possible cryovolcanism
Evidence suggests a subsurface ocean of liquid water

faq.question: What are the bright spots on Ceres?
faq.answer: The brightest features in Occator Crater are deposits of sodium carbonate salt — the largest such deposits in the solar system outside Earth. They likely formed when briny subsurface water reached the surface through cracks and evaporated, leaving salt behind.

faq.question: Could Ceres harbor life?
faq.answer: It's unlikely but not impossible. Ceres has liquid water, organic molecules, and heat from radioactive decay — three ingredients for life. However, the ocean is probably very cold and saline.
